svg.title: Site and symptom: one anatomical schematic shared by three tumours, every line labelled with its tumour
svg.desc: Schematic on how the site of a benign brain tumour maps to symptoms, with one hand-drawn anatomical diagram shared by all three tumours. The anatomical drawing is hand-drawn, not to scale and not an anatomical reference; its eleven numbered points are coloured by tumour — gold for meningioma, green for vestibular schwannoma, blue for pituitary adenoma. The numbered points are: 1 convexity (meningioma); 2 parasagittal and falx (meningioma); 3 anterior fossa, including the olfactory groove and orbitofrontal region (meningioma); 4 sphenoid wing and middle fossa (meningioma); 5 tuberculum sellae, against the visual pathway (meningioma); 6 the pituitary gland in the sella (pituitary adenoma); 7 petroclival region (meningioma); 8 internal auditory canal and cerebellopontine angle (vestibular schwannoma); 9 posterior fossa and around the torcula (meningioma); 10 intraventricular (meningioma); 11 spinal cord, which is a separate site code (meningioma). The first section gives the distribution of meningioma by site, as ranges rather than single numbers, from a review pooling several series: convexity 20 to 37%; parasagittal 13 to 22%, of which falx 5%; skull base 43 to 51% in total, broken down into anterior skull base 10 to 20%, sphenoid wing and middle fossa 9 to 36%, and posterior fossa 6 to 15%, of which cerebellopontine angle 2 to 11% and petroclival under 1% to 9%; intraventricular 1 to 5%; orbit under 1% to 2%; spinal cord 7 to 12%. The figure notes that the spinal row needs care, because the US brain tumour registry counts the spinal meninges as a separate site code, so the denominator is not the same. Site is related to grade as well, still for meningioma: the same review states that grade 1 meningiomas are more often at the skull base and higher-grade ones more often at the convexity, parasagittally, on the falx, at the torcula and intraventricularly; a pathological analysis of 2,608 meningiomas points the same way, with the Ki-67 proliferation index of skull base meningiomas significantly lower than that of convexity meningiomas, which holds after stratifying within the same grade. The second section gives what meningiomas present with: headache 33.3 to 36.7%, focal cranial nerve deficit 28.8 to 31.3%, seizure 16.9 to 24.6%, cognitive change 14.4%, weakness 11.1%, no symptoms 9.4%; and skull base meningiomas more often present with a neurological deficit, non-skull-base ones more often with a seizure. It then goes site by site, each line labelled as meningioma and only meningioma. Anterior fossa (olfactory groove, orbitofrontal, anterior falx): often already large at diagnosis, with impaired vision 54%, headache 48%, loss of smell 40% and seizure 20%, sometimes with disinhibited changes in personality; these percentages come from a population already large at diagnosis and cannot be applied to a small incidental tumour. Parasagittal: can grow quite large before causing symptoms, often presenting with a Jacksonian seizure starting in the leg or with headache, and in the advanced stage characteristically papilloedema and a homonymous hemianopia. Tuberculum sellae: usually presents with insidious unilateral visual loss followed by a scotoma in the other eye — one eye gradually dims, then the other. Lateral sphenoid wing: often painless unilateral proptosis followed by ipsilateral visual loss. Petroclival: gait ataxia and cranial neuropathy, for example trigeminal involvement. Anterior clinoid: visual disturbance of various kinds, cranial nerve palsy, proptosis. Posterior fossa: may cause obstructive hydrocephalus, presenting as papilloedema and morning headache. Around the torcula: local occipital pain, papilloedema, an ipsilateral visual field defect, with ataxia and nystagmus. Spinal cord: most often thoracic, presenting as slowly progressive spastic paraparesis, sometimes with radicular or nocturnal pain, with the cervical spine and craniocervical junction second commonest. Against bone: local hyperostosis, which the review says is almost invariably a sign of bone invasion by meningioma cells and which can cause a swelling and pain. The third section states that the cerebellopontine angle is not only vestibular schwannoma, in three boxes. Meningioma: 2 to 11% of meningiomas are in the cerebellopontine angle, the same row as in the table above. Vestibular schwannoma: the Danish national cohort divides it into intracanalicular tumours and tumours extending into the cerebellopontine angle, whose natural history differs and whose statistics are kept separate, so a report saying "cerebellopontine angle lesion" has not yet named the disease. Epidermoid cyst: this is a site where they occur too, and the series of 17 cases was of epidermoid cysts here. The fourth section covers when new unilateral hearing loss should be imaged, from the CNS 2018 screening guideline for vestibular schwannoma: on the audiogram, MRI screening is recommended for people with an interaural difference of 10 dB or more at two or more adjacent frequencies, or of 15 dB or more at a single frequency, to reduce the number of undiagnosed vestibular schwannomas; to reduce the number of scans that diagnose nothing, this can be narrowed to an interaural difference of 15 dB or more at the single frequency of 3000 Hz. The same guideline sets out the unflattering side: MRI done for asymmetrical tinnitus diagnoses a vestibular schwannoma in under 1% of cases and MRI done for sudden sensorineural hearing loss in under 3%, and both numbers support "it should be looked for" and "the chance of finding it is low" at once. Taiwan has its own wording: item 100901030 of the National Health Insurance review guidance lists ten clinical situations in which CT or MRI may reasonably be arranged for an otological patient, including auditory brainstem response suggesting retrocochlear disease, unilateral hearing loss of more than 65 dB at 2 to 4 kHz, poor word recognition scores, focal neurological signs, pulsatile tinnitus and unusual vertigo or central nystagmus; its threshold is not the same ruler as the guideline above, one counting the difference between the ears in dB and the other the loss in one ear, and both are set out without ranking. The figure states that this line is written for the doctor who orders the scan and is not for comparing your own audiogram against. The fifth section covers the direction a pituitary adenoma grows. Upward is commonest: the diaphragma sellae and its opening are a weak barrier to expansion and the tumour may compress and damage the optic nerves and chiasm; where the chiasm sits posteriorly the tumour grows forward under the frontal lobe, and where it sits anteriorly, backward into the third ventricle and hypothalamus. Downward causes remodelling, enlargement and bone resorption of the sella, leaving a route into the sphenoid sinus. Forward means invasion of the planum sphenoidale, the undersurface of the frontal lobe and the ethmoid sinuses. Backward means expansion into the interpeduncular cistern and against the brainstem. Laterally means expansion into or invasion of the cavernous sinus. Invasion is not rare: up to 35% of adenoma types show gross invasion, and the proportion is higher for macroadenomas. This is why the Endocrine Society incidentaloma guideline requires visual field testing for anyone whose lesion abuts or compresses the optic nerves and chiasm, at 6 months and then annually during follow-up. A Swedish study of 654 people is clear about what patients report first: non-functioning adenomas, headache and visual disturbance; prolactinoma, irregular periods and headache; acromegaly, a change in appearance and snoring; Cushing's disease, weight gain and fatigue. The sixth section states that site mattering does not mean size can be ignored, with both lines labelled meningioma: in a meta-analysis of 2,130 people a diameter of 3 cm or more was a factor associated with developing symptoms during active monitoring, but its 95% confidence interval is wide enough that only the direction, not a multiple, can be stated; and in a prognostic model of 441 people and 459 incidental meningiomas the hazard ratio for increasing tumour volume was 2.17, 95% confidence interval 1.53 to 3.09, a hazard ratio being the ratio of the rate at which events occur in the two groups, so size is one of the parameters in the model and not something that can be discarded. The other way round has to be said too: however typical the site, some people feel nothing at all, and that 9.4% of meningiomas with no symptoms is exactly how they are stumbled upon; the same site can also be a different grade, and the EANO guideline states plainly that there is considerable individual variation between grade and clinical course. The figure closes on the reading that is ruled out: this is not a chart for placing yourself on. All the correspondences above are at the level of populations, and reasoning backwards from a symptom to a site, or forwards from a site to what will happen to you, goes wrong. What the site really settles is three things: who takes the case first, since touching the visual pathway brings in ophthalmology and endocrinology while sitting in the internal auditory canal brings in neuro-otology; what else to measure in the first round, since visual fields, hearing and hormones each apply to one of them and the one that applies must not be left out; and which direction to watch on follow-up, since growing upward and growing laterally are watched for different things. At the next clinic visit the questions to ask are: which structure is mine abutting or pressing on, what should be added to the first round of tests because of that site, and which direction should the follow-up scan look at?

g.text: WHERE IT SITS, AND WHAT THAT CHANGES
Change the site and the whole set of symptoms changes
At the same 2 cm, one on the surface of the frontal lobe may go unnoticed for ten years, while one on the tuberculum sellae may already
be taking the sight of one eye.
What this figure settles is who takes the case first, what else to measure in the first round, and which direction to watch on follow-up. It is
not a chart for placing yourself on.
One schematic, shared by all three tumours
Hand-drawn, not to scale, and not an anatomical reference. Every number carries a tumour label — the same site can grow different tumours.
front (face)
back (occiput)
convexity | meningioma
parasagittal and falx | meningioma
anterior fossa (olfactory groove, orbitofrontal) | meningioma
sphenoid wing and middle fossa | meningioma
tuberculum sellae (against the visual pathway) | meningioma
sella: the pituitary gland | pituitary adenoma
petroclival region | meningioma
internal auditory canal and cerebellopontine angle | vestibular schwannoma
posterior fossa and around the torcula | meningioma
intraventricular | meningioma
spinal cord (a separate site code) | meningioma
The colour is the tumour: gold for meningioma, green for vestibular schwannoma, blue for pituitary adenoma.
Meningiomas have a distribution by site
A review pooling several series gives ranges rather than single numbers, copied out below. This whole section is about meningioma.
meningioma
convexity
parasagittal (of which falx 5%)
skull base, total
anterior skull base
sphenoid wing and middle fossa
posterior fossa
of which cerebellopontine angle
of which petroclival
under 1% to 9%
intraventricular
1 to 5%
orbit
under 1% to 2%
spinal cord
Watch the spinal row: the US brain tumour registry counts the spinal meninges as a separate site code, so the denominator is not the same.
Site is related to grade as well (still meningioma)
The same review is direct about it: grade 1 meningiomas are more often at the skull base, and higher-grade ones more often at the convexity, parasagittally, on the falx, at the
torcula and intraventricularly. A pathological analysis of 2,608 meningiomas points the same way: the Ki-67 proliferation index of skull base meningiomas is significantly
lower than that of convexity meningiomas, and this holds after stratifying within the same grade.
What meningiomas present with, and how each site behaves
Every line below is about meningioma and only meningioma — the same site can grow a different tumour, so this set of correspondences cannot be carried over to another
one.
meningioma
headache
focal cranial nerve deficit
seizure
cognitive change
weakness
no symptoms
And skull base meningiomas more often present with a neurological deficit, non-skull-base ones more often with a seizure.
anterior fossa (olfactory groove,
orbitofrontal, anterior falx)
Often already large at diagnosis; impaired vision 54%, headache 48%, loss of smell 40%, seizure 20%, sometimes with disinhibited changes
in personality. These percentages come from a population already large at diagnosis and cannot be applied to a small incidental tumour.
parasagittal
Can grow quite large before causing symptoms; often presents with a Jacksonian seizure starting in the leg, or with headache; in the
advanced stage characteristically papilloedema and a homonymous hemianopia.
tuberculum sellae
"Usually presents with insidious unilateral visual loss, followed by a scotoma in the other eye" — note the order: one eye gradually dims,
then the other. That is the meningioma pattern.
lateral sphenoid wing
Often presents with painless unilateral proptosis, followed by ipsilateral visual loss.
petroclival
Gait ataxia and cranial neuropathy, for example trigeminal involvement.
anterior clinoid
Visual disturbance of various kinds, cranial nerve palsy, proptosis.
posterior fossa
May cause obstructive hydrocephalus, presenting as papilloedema and morning headache.
around the torcula
Local occipital pain, papilloedema, an ipsilateral visual field defect, with ataxia and nystagmus.
spinal cord
Most often thoracic, presenting as slowly progressive spastic paraparesis, sometimes with radicular or nocturnal pain; the cervical
spine and craniocervical junction are the second commonest.
against bone
Local hyperostosis, which the review says is "almost invariably a sign of bone invasion by meningioma cells", and which can cause a
swelling and pain.
The cerebellopontine angle is not only vestibular schwannoma
meningioma
2 to 11% of meningiomas are in the cerebellopontine
angle (the same row as in the table above).
vestibular schwannoma
The Danish national cohort divides vestibular
schwannoma into intracanalicular tumours and
tumours extending into the cerebellopontine angle;
the natural history differs, and the statistics are
kept separate.
So when a report says "cerebellopontine angle
lesion", that sentence has not yet named the
disease.
epidermoid cyst
This is a site where they occur too — the series of
17 cases was of epidermoid cysts here.
When new unilateral hearing loss should be imaged
vestibular schwannoma
CNS 2018 screening guideline (vestibular schwannoma)
On the audiogram, MRI screening is recommended for people with an interaural difference of 10 dB or more at two or more adjacent frequencies, or of 15 dB
or more at a single frequency, in order to reduce the number of undiagnosed vestibular schwannomas.
To reduce the number of scans that diagnose nothing, this can be narrowed to screening only those with an interaural difference of 15 dB or more at the single
frequency of 3000 Hz.
The same guideline sets out the unflattering side as well: MRI done for asymmetrical tinnitus diagnoses a vestibular schwannoma in under 1% of cases, and MRI done for sudden
sensorineural hearing loss in under 3%. Both numbers support "it should be looked for" and "the chance of finding it is low" at once.
Taiwan has its own wording: item 100901030 of the National Health Insurance review guidance lists ten clinical situations in which "CT or MRI may reasonably be arranged for an
otological patient", including auditory brainstem response suggesting retrocochlear disease, unilateral hearing loss of more than 65 dB at 2 to 4 kHz, poor word recognition
scores, focal neurological signs, pulsatile tinnitus and unusual vertigo or central nystagmus. Its threshold is not the same ruler as the guideline above — one counts the difference
between the ears in dB, the other the loss in one ear in dB. Both are set out, without ranking.
This line is written for the doctor who orders the scan. It is not for comparing your own audiogram against.
Pituitary adenoma: the direction it grows decides what you notice first
pituitary adenoma
upward (commonest)
The diaphragma sellae and its opening are a weak barrier to expansion, and the tumour may compress and damage the optic nerves and
chiasm; where the chiasm sits posteriorly the tumour grows forward under the frontal lobe, and where it sits anteriorly, backward into the
third ventricle and hypothalamus.
downward
Remodelling, enlargement and bone resorption of the sella, leaving a route into the sphenoid sinus.
forward
Invasion of the planum sphenoidale, the undersurface of the frontal lobe and the ethmoid sinuses.
backward
Expansion into the interpeduncular cistern and against the brainstem.
laterally
Expansion into or invasion of the cavernous sinus.
Invasion is not rare: "up to 35% of adenoma types show gross invasion", and the proportion is higher for macroadenomas.
Which is why the Endocrine Society incidentaloma guideline requires visual field testing for anyone whose lesion abuts or compresses the optic nerves and chiasm, at 6 months
and then annually during follow-up.
A Swedish study of 654 people is clear about what patients report first: non-functioning adenomas, headache and visual disturbance; prolactinoma, irregular periods and headache;
acromegaly, a change in appearance and snoring; Cushing's disease, weight gain and fatigue.
Site matters, which does not mean size can be ignored
meningioma
meningioma: 3 cm or more in diameter
In a meta-analysis of 2,130 people, a diameter of 3 cm or more was a factor associated
with developing symptoms during active monitoring, but its 95% confidence interval is
wide enough that only the direction, not a multiple, can be stated.
meningioma
meningioma: hazard ratio 2.17 for increasing tumour volume
In a prognostic model of 441 people and 459 incidental meningiomas, 95% confidence
interval 1.53 to 3.09; a hazard ratio is the ratio of the rate at which events occur in the
two groups. Size is one of the parameters in the model, not something that can be
discarded.
The other way round has to be said too: however typical the site, some people feel nothing at all — that 9.4% of meningiomas with no symptoms is exactly how they are stumbled
upon. The same site can also be a different grade; the EANO guideline states plainly that there is considerable individual variation between grade and clinical course.
This is not a chart for placing yourself on
All the correspondences above are at the level of populations. Reasoning backwards from a symptom to a site, or forwards from a site to what will happen to you,
goes wrong.
What the site really settles is three things: who takes the case first (touching the visual pathway brings in ophthalmology and endocrinology; sitting in the internal
auditory canal brings in neuro-otology); what else to measure in the first round (visual fields, hearing, hormones — the one that applies must not be left out); and
which direction to watch on follow-up (growing upward and growing laterally are watched for different things).
At the next clinic visit, put it like this: which structure is mine abutting or pressing on? Because of that site, what should be added to the first round of tests? Which
direction should the follow-up scan look at?
Schematic. The anatomical drawing is hand-drawn, not to scale, and is not reproduced from any paper or atlas; the numbers are redrawn from Ogasawara 2021, CBTRUS
2017–2021, Broechner 2026, Czernicki 2016, Reznitsky 2021, the CNS 2018 otologic and audiologic screening guideline, Melmed 2022, the Endocrine Society 2011 pituitary
incidentaloma guideline, Forsgren 2025, Islim 2019, Islim 2020, the EANO 2021 meningioma guideline and the National Health Insurance review guidance; the cohorts, designs
and endpoints of the underlying sources differ, so the data points must not be compared directly.
